title: The ladder of practice (12.8–12.12)
hook: Krishna gives a path with a step for every kind of day

segments.voice: Yesterday: avyakta, form or formless? Arjuna asked which kind of devotee is best, the one who loves God with a face or the one who seeks the formless. Your line was either way. Both arrive. Today, what to do when neither feels possible. Day two hundred two.

A good physical therapist, the first week after an injury, says: today, walk to the door and back. You can't. Fine, they say. Stand up and sit down five times. You can't do that either. Fine. Squeeze this ball. Nobody leaves the room with nothing to do. There's always a smaller step that still counts. Chapter twelve of the Gita has a stretch that works exactly like that. Krishna has just said the goal. Then, instead of repeating it louder, he starts handing Arjuna smaller and smaller steps.
screen: `CAN'T WALK TO THE DOOR?` → `STAND UP AND SIT DOWN.` → `THERE'S ALWAYS A SMALLER STEP.`

segments.voice: Here's the ladder, verses eight through eleven, told from the top. The highest rung: fix your mind on me, let your understanding rest in me, and you will live in me. That's the whole goal in one sentence. Then verse nine: if you can't hold your mind steady on me, then seek me through practice. The Sanskrit is abhyasa, practice, the repeating, coming back again and again. We met it in chapter six with the restless mind. Verse ten: if you can't even practice, then make your work for my sake. Do your ordinary actions as an offering, and you'll reach perfection that way. And verse eleven, the bottom rung: if you can't do even that, then take refuge in me, keep yourself in check, and give up the fruit of all your actions. Just let go of how it turns out. Four rungs, and each one below the top begins the same way: if you can't. There's no scolding in it. No verse says if you can't, you've failed. Each one says, then here's the next thing. Then verse twelve turns the ladder around in a way that surprises people. Knowledge is better than practice, it says. Meditation is better than knowledge. And giving up the fruit of action is better than meditation, because peace follows that letting go right away. The lowest rung turns out to hold something the higher ones need. Commentators read this verse in different ways and don't rank the steps alike. What the text itself does is plain: it leaves no one without a step, however busy or scattered. That's the word today: the ladder of practice.
screen: `FIX YOUR MIND ON ME.` · `IF YOU CAN'T, PRACTICE.` · `IF YOU CAN'T, WORK AS OFFERING.` · `IF YOU CAN'T, LET GO OF THE FRUIT.` · then, large: `THE LADDER OF PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and try the top rung first. Rest your attention on whatever you hold most dear, a name, a face, or just stillness. When it slips, and it will, drop one rung. Come back to the breath, again and again. That's practice. If even that feels too much today, pick one thing you'll do after the bell and quietly dedicate it. And if you can't manage that, just let go of how today will turn out. Any rung counts. The bell holds the time.

Abhyasa, practice, the coming back again and again. Gita twelve, eight to twelve: fix your mind on the divine; if you can't, practice; if you can't, work as offering; if you can't, let go of the fruit.
Your line: find the smaller rung. Today, when something good feels too big to do, don't quit it. Take that smaller step instead. Day two hundred two.

screen: `DAY 202 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE ONE DEAR TO ME.`

howItsDone: Many Hindus read Gita 12.8–12.12 as permission to begin wherever they are: some meditate, some keep a daily practice like japa, and many simply offer their ordinary work and let go of the result.

match.prompt: the rungs of the ladder — tap the pairs.
pairs: if you can't, work for my sake
if you can't, give up the fruit

myth: in chapter 12, the lower rungs are scolded as failures
each rung below the top starts 'if you can't' and simply offers the next step. no verse scolds.
verse 12 says giving up the fruit is better than meditation
it says peace follows that letting go right away.
abhyasa means practice: coming back again and again
the same word the Gita used for the restless mind in chapter six.

fork.setup: you're Arjuna. you've heard 'fix your mind on me' and you know you can't hold it. what does Krishna say next?
options: then you're not ready for this path.
fork.reveal: then practice. each lower rung begins with 'if you can't', and none of them sends anyone away.

original.note: Sanskrit: abhyasa, practice, repeated effort; the rung below 'fix your mind on me' in Gita 12.9.

trapdoor: what you thought: spiritual life is for people with lots of time and a calm mind.
what it means: the Gita gives a ladder with a rung for every kind of day, down to simply letting go of the result.

what a scholar hears: 12.12 ranks knowledge, meditation and relinquishing the fruit (karma-phala-tyaga) in a way commentators have read differently; the text says peace follows relinquishment immediately.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 12.8–12.11 (the ladder: mind, practice, work, relinquishing fruit)
Bhagavad Gita 12.12 (the ranking; peace follows relinquishment)
Bhagavad Gita 6.35 (abhyasa and the restless mind)

notes: All verses paraphrased. Check the order and wording of 12.8–12.12.
'Commentators... don't agree on exactly how to rank the steps' in 12.12: confirm this is fair (Shankara and Ramanuja read the verse differently).
The practice keeps a 'dedicate one act' step phrased as an invitation, with no prayer text.
